pg:https://www.newser.com/story/400114/g.desc: Plea covers Rockstar Games breach and earlier Lapsus$ cyberattacks
paras: A British hacker who used an Amazon Fire Stick in a Travelodge to breach Rockstar Games has now admitted to the crime in court, the BBC reports. Arion Kurtaj, 21, pleaded guilty Monday at Woolwich Crown Court to hacking the maker of Grand Theft Auto 6 in 2022, stealing 90 clips showing nearly an hour of unreleased gameplay and threatening to leak the game's source code unless contacted on Telegram. He posted the material online after the company refused to engage, an incident Rockstar says cost about $5 million and exposed closely guarded game details.

Prosecutors called Kurtaj a key figure in the Lapsus$ hacking group, tying him to earlier attacks on BT/EE, Revolut, and Uber, plus crypto thefts, causing roughly $13 million in damages. Initially deemed unfit for trial due to severe autism and sent to a secure hospital, he was later reassessed as fit and transferred to prison. He also admitted to assaults on workers while he was in custody and will be sentenced later. The news comes as fans eagerly await the release of GTA 6 on Thursday; CNN calls it "the biggest entertainment event of the year." pg:https://theconversation.com/nasas-voy.desc: The spacecraft is travelling through interstellar space, around 16 billion miles from Earth.
paras: Nasa’s Voyager 1 spacecraft, launched in 1977, has marked an extraordinary milestone. At 10:16:07 GMT (05:16:07 EST) on November 18, 2026, it reached a distance of one light day from Earth.

One light day is the distance that light can travel in a vacuum in 24 hours and is equal to about 16 billion miles (about 26 billion kilometres). A light year, often used to measure distances from Earth to astronomical objects like other stars, is the distance light can travel in space in one year.

For some perspective, the Artemis II mission set a new record for the greatest distance from Earth travelled by humans, at 252,756 miles, in April 2026. It takes light just over 1.3 seconds to travel this distance. Voyager 1 is now more than 63,000 times further away than the human distance record set by Artemis II.

Also included will be objects from Swift’s record-setting Eras Tour (2023-2024), including a custom red Alberta Ferretti gown worn during the folklore and evermore sets on the global stadium outing.

Among the other objects on display will be the bejeweled Midnights bodysuit designed by Zuhair Murad, as well as the tinsel-fringed jacket from the show’s “Karma” finale and a recreation of the “Fortnight” video set from The Tortured Poets Department era featuring Swift’s Victorian-inspired dress and typewriter.

The Boston museum will be the only venue for the exhibit, which will also include a number of Swift’s signature instruments, including a Deering banjo from the Speak Now tour, a mandolin from the “Willow” video and the shell of a pink-and-gold piano from Swift’s “Lover” performance at the 2019 American Music Awards.

pg:https://theconversation.com/nasas-voy.desc: The probe has explored both the solar system and the interstellar medium beyond during its decades-long journey.
paras: In the summer of 2027, the Voyager 1 and Voyager 2 spacecraft will each reach a milestone in time. On Sept. 5 and Aug. 20, respectively, they will each have spent 50 years in space.

During their journeys, they first explored the planets of the outer solar system, then traveled to the edge of the solar system. Eventually, they passed into the interstellar medium: the space between stars. Although not the first spacecraft ever launched, these are now the two oldest spacecraft still operating.

But before the spacecraft hit their semicentennial, Voyager 1 will also reach a milestone in distance. On Nov. 18, 2026, at 5:16 a.m. EST, Voyager 1 will become the first human-built object of any kind to reach a distance of one light-day from Earth. At that point, it will have traveled about 16 billion miles (26 billion kilometers), more than four times the distance from the Sun to Pluto. Afterward, it will take light, including communication signals, 24 hours to travel between the spacecraft and Earth.

pg:https://www.cbc.ca/news/science/voyag.desc: Voyager 1, already the farthest a human-made object has ever gone, has crossed the arbitrary but important threshold of a light day. It now takes 24 hours to send a message to the probe, now in interstellar space.
paras: Launched in 1977, Voyager 1 was meant to study the gas giants of our solar system, Jupiter and Saturn. But by 1998, it continued on past them, becoming the farthest human-made object ever. It reached interstellar space — the region just outside the sun’s magnetic influence known as the heliopause — back in 2012, at a distance of 18 billion kilometres. Now, it’s more than 26 billion kilometres away.

Arguably, being a “light day” away is an arbitrary threshold, as there’s no new physical boundary or change to Voyager 1 itself. But experts say it’s remarkable because it’s still plugging along on its mission while communicating with Earth.

Voyager 1’s power is generated by the heat from the natural decay of plutonium. As that power has dwindled over nearly half a century, most of its science instruments have been shut down, the latest being the LCEP, which measured low-energy charged particles. There are two instruments that still work, one for measuring plasma waves and the other for magnetic fields.

pg:https://mashable.com/tech/faa-ground-.desc: The federal agency has directed blame towards its contractor, but a new report questions who is truly at fault.
paras: The FAA official oversaw the work, tested it, and signed off on it, according to the Post's report. The fact that an FAA official greenlit the work complicates Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy's efforts to point fingers at L3Harris Technologies, a tech services provider and contractor tasked with updating the wires in Arkansas and leading the FAA's fiber-optic upgrades. Duffy said on Saturday that his agency is looking into whether "incompetence" by L3Harris led to the 4.5-hour ground stop.

Responding to the Post's request for comment, the FAA pointed to statements Duffy made on Tuesday in a news conference at the Capitol. During the conference, Duffy said that he wanted L3Harris to "hire better minds" for the wire replacement work and was considering bringing in new contractors to help.

pg:https://www.nbcnews.com/politics/cong.desc: Despite grumbling from some on the left, no one ran against Jeffries, who guided House Democrats to their largest majority in 35 years. A full House vote will be held on Jan. 3.

But Jeffries asked for a recorded vote to give his rank-and-file members an opportunity to voice their support or opposition — something he said the Democratic Caucus did when it returned Nancy Pelosi to the speaker’s office after the 2018 midterm elections amid calls for a new generation of leadership.

Jeffries campaigned across the country in recent months and helped Democrats win what NBC News projects will be 259 seats — the largest majority in 35 years and well more than the 218 votes he will need to be elected speaker on the House floor on Jan. 3.

pg:https://www.theguardian.com/film/2026.desc: With the UK release of You Can See Everything looming, now’s an ideal time to get up to speed on the bizarre, puckish and very meta comedic oeuvre of its star
paras: The three-hour documentary You Can See Everything – co-directed by and starring Fielder – opens in the UK on Friday, having already become an unlikely cultural phenomenon and box office sensation in the US. The film follows disgraced Theranos founder Elizabeth Holmes in the weeks leading up to her beginning a prison sentence for defrauding investors; what emerges is a profound meditation on the nature of truth and the fundamental unknowability of other human beings. To view the film as being simply about the Theranos scandal is akin to considering Casablanca merely a movie about a nightclub. And, as one might expect given Fielder’s background, it’s hilarious.

The show went far beyond its original premise and ended up occupying a position on the Venn diagram where comedy overlaps with performance art. One third season episode, Smokers Allowed, seemed to mark a turning point in Fielder’s career. Over an extraordinary 21 minutes, he was tasked with reviving the fortunes of a bar. After discovering punters would be allowed to smoke in the establishment so long as events were presented as a “play” (for an audience of two), he filmed a standard night at the bar and hired actors to recreate the “events” verbatim – a ploy that seems to have more in common with Charlie Kaufman’s autofiction than Trigger Happy TV.

The first series of The Rehearsal saw Fielder attempting to aid a woman contemplating motherhood; while the second saw him effect real change in regard to global aviation safety, with an attempt to cut down on the number of airline crashes. Not bad for a man who, just over a decade earlier, opened the first episode of Nathan for You with a segment involving poo flavoured frozen yoghurt.

pg:https://www.wsws.org/en/articles/2026.desc: The Pan American Health Organization announced Tuesday that the United States, along with Mexico and Bolivia, has lost its measles elimination status, as two more measles-associated deaths bring the 2026 US toll to 10.
paras: Noel Brewer, chair of an independent US committee that presented findings on the country’s outbreaks to PAHO, told the Wall Street Journal, “Runaway measles outbreaks in the United States, as well as the needless deaths, are all due to low measles vaccination coverage. We’ve gotten comfortable letting children be stopped by a deadly disease and die from it.”

In the past week, two more measles-associated deaths have raised the toll reported by state health departments in 2026 to 10. On November 13, the Pennsylvania Department of Health confirmed the state’s seventh, an unvaccinated resident of Montour County, whose age the department did not release. Montour joins Lancaster County, with three deaths; Jefferson County, with two; and Mifflin County, with one. The same day, the Wisconsin Department of Health Services and the Grant County Health Department announced a pediatric measles-associated death, the state’s second in eight days, with no further details released. The escalation is without precedent since elimination.

In the 21 years from 2004 through 2024, only a single person died of measles in the United States, a Washington state woman in 2015. Since the current surge began in 2025, 13 people have died, three in 2025 and 10 this year, five of them in November alone. The last time the United States recorded as many as 10 measles deaths in a single year was 1991, at the end of a resurgence that produced some 55,000 cases and more than 120 deaths from 1989 through 1991.

paras: The robotic probe, launched in 1977, was calculated by NASA to have reached a light-day from Earth, the distance that light travels in 24 hours — about 16 billion miles — on Wednesday at 5:16 a.m. ET.

pg:https://www.engadget.com/2320267/nasa.desc: It now takes 24 hours to send a message to Voyager 1, as it reaches a distance that’s one light-day away from our planet.
paras: NASA Add Engadget on Google: Google Discover If NASA's estimates are correct, Voyager 1 is already one light-day away from our planet. NASA expects it to have reached that milestone at 5:16:07 AM Eastern time today, November 18. One light-day is the distance a particle of light can travel in a day. Since radio waves travel at the speed of light, it now takes 24 hours to send a command to the probe and 24 hours to get a message back. That's why NASA won't be able to confirm exactly what time it reached one light-day away until tomorrow, when the probe's message arrives.

Voyager 1 headed to space in 1977 as part of NASA's program to study not just our Solar System, but also interstellar space. It was launched 16 days after Voyager 2, but it has since traveled farther than its twin and any other probe we've sent out. Voyager 1 reached interstellar space — that's the region between star systems — back in 2012, before Voyager 2 did. It suffered technical glitches, and NASA had to shut down some of its features to keep it going despite the diminishing plutonium in its generator. But it's still around and hasn't stopped its journey.

After traveling for 49 years, two months and 11 days, it's now believed to be about 16 billion miles from our planet—and it's not done yet. Voyager 1 is headed toward a star called Gliese 445, about 17 light-years from Earth in the Ursa Minor constellation. In terms of space distances, that's not so far away. However, none of us would be here by the time it reaches that goal: It's expected to pass within 1.7 light-years of Gliese 445 in 40,000 years.

pg:https://www.wired.com/story/voyager-1.desc: The spacecraft stores data on an eight-track tape, but it’s managed to stay in contact with scientists for decades. Now, it’s the first human-made object to travel a light-day away from Earth.
paras: Voyager 1, launched in September 1977 toward the outer planets of our solar system, achieved a historic milestone on Wednesday: It became the first human-made object to reach one light-day from Earth. The spacecraft is so far away, that by the time its light reaches Earth, it comes from the spacecraft as it existed one day in the past. The achievement is one researchers hadn’t planned on, and yet, as Voyager 1 wades deeper into uncharted stretches of the galaxy, it continues sending back valuable scientific information.

For Fran Bagenal, a planetary scientist at the University of Colorado, Boulder, who began working with Voyager 1 as a graduate student during its earliest years, the occasion is a momentous technological feat. “What's exciting is the fact that we have a spacecraft that was built in the mid ’70s that is still working,” she says. “Storing data on an eight-track tape that’s working on a spacecraft after 50 years—I mean, it’s amazing.”

Even as Voyager 1 approaches its 50-year anniversary next September, and its end of mission perhaps not long after that, the spacecraft is still checking items off its laundry list of scientific achievements. The spacecraft—alongside its twin, Voyager 2—was originally intended to take advantage of a rare planetary alignment to observe the outer planets.

pg:https://arstechnica.com/health/2026/1.desc: Measles became endemic in the US months ago—and it's only accelerating.
paras: After the announcement Tuesday, public health experts, doctors, and political leaders decried the dramatic backslide for the US, calling it “shameful” and a “national embarrassment.” News articles point to the staggering vertical rise of measles cases this year, currently over 5,400 cases, more than any other year since 1991. An explosive measles outbreak in Pennsylvania accounts for over 1,500 of those cases. There have been 10 confirmed deaths across three states, several deaths just in the last week.

But the measles data that caused the US to lose its status—the bits of it that are public at least—paint a darker picture of where the US is in its rematch with measles, the most contagious virus known on Earth. For one thing, almost none of the data from this year—the cases, the explosive Pennsylvania outbreak, the deaths—factored in to the loss. It was lost earlier. What’s happening now is a runaway epidemic.

The US measles elimination status is a designation granted by the Pan American Health Organization (PAHO), which is a regional division of the World Health Organization. Last week a committee of experts assembled by the PAHO, called the RVC, met to review measles data for countries across the region, including the US. (RVC is short for the Measles, Rubella and Congenital Rubella Syndrome Elimination Regional Monitoring and Re-Verification Commission.)

LOS ANGELES, Nov. 18 (Xinhua) -- NASA's Voyager 1 spacecraft reached a distance of one light-day from Earth on Wednesday, becoming the first human-made object to travel so far into space, NASA said on its official Voyager mission website.

According to NASA's calculations, the milestone occurred at 5:16:07 a.m. Eastern Time on Wednesday. One light-day is the distance a particle of light can travel in 24 hours, equivalent to about 26 billion kilometers.

Launched in 1977 to fly by Jupiter and Saturn, Voyager 1 has been traveling through space for nearly 50 years. Its twin spacecraft, Voyager 2, followed a different trajectory through the solar system to explore Uranus and Neptune. Voyager 2 is expected to reach the one-light-day distance from Earth in November 2035, NASA said.

pg:https://www.theguardian.com/commentis.desc: Since the spacecraft’s 1977 launch, our wonderful and terrible species has done great damage to our planet. Voyager has offered us a clear view of ourselves
paras: Since the spacecraft’s 1977 launch, our wonderful and terrible species has done great damage to our planet. Voyager has offered us a clear view of ourselves
Imagine traveling nonstop for 49 years, alone in the dark with no destination in sight, powered by curiosity and engineering.

Further imagine making that journey not at bullet train or jet plane speed, but much faster: at 37,800 miles per hour, free from friction in a vast sea of cold, soundless space, bombarded by radiation and cosmic rays yet still able to communicate with folks back home.

pg:https://www.wral.com/weather/voyager-.desc: Nearly 50 years after launch, Voyager 1 has reached a distance of one light-day from Earth, continuing to send scientific data across 16 billion miles
paras: Voyager 1 reaches a milestone nearly 50 years in the making: One light-day from Earth Nearly 50 years after launch, Voyager 1 has reached a distance of one light-day from Earth, continuing to send scientific data across 16 billion miles Posted 11/18/2026, 4:12:17 PM By Tony Rice, NASA Ambassador Nearly five decades after leaving Earth, NASA's Voyager 1 has traveled so far that radios signal take an entire day to reach it and it to reach back out to Earth. No human-made object has ever been this far away.

It crossed the one-light-day milestone.Wednesday morning, November 18, becoming the first human-made object to travel that far from Earth. At 5:16 a.m. Eastern time, the spacecraft passed a distance of 16.094 billion miles, or 25.902 billion kilometers. A light-day is the distance light travels in 24 hours. At approximately 186,000 miles per second, that works out to more than 16 billion miles.

A signal weaker than you can imagine Getting data back to Earth from a light day away is engineering accomplishment in itself. By the time Voyager's radio signal reaches Earth, its power has faded to approximately -160 dBm, or about 100 attowatts. An attowatt is one quintillionth of a watt.

pg:https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/1.desc: The ICJ rules on The Gambia’s genocide case against Myanmar. Here’s what’s at stake for the Rohingya.
paras: On Thursday, November 19, the International Court of Justice (ICJ) in The Hague will deliver its verdict in a landmark case brought by The Gambia, accusing Myanmar of genocide against the Rohingya ethnic minority.

The ruling, which will be final and cannot be appealed, comes seven years after The Gambia filed its case with the backing of the Organisation of Islamic Cooperation (OIC), and more than nine years after a military crackdown in Myanmar’s Rakhine State forced more than 740,000 Rohingya to flee to neighbouring Bangladesh.
The Rohingya are a mostly Muslim ethnic minority who have lived for centuries in Rakhine State, western Myanmar.

Russian authorities have launched a criminal investigation into what they are calling a "terrorist attack." The Kerch Strait bridge is considered one of Russian President Vladimir Putin's most prestigious projects. Its construction began after Russia's 2014 annexation of the Ukrainian Crimea peninsula, an act considered illegal under international law. The Kerch Bridge was completed four years later.

For Ukraine, the bridge is a hated symbol of Russian arrogance and colonial thinking. Ukraine has previously declared that the bridge across the Kerch strait, built eight years ago, is illegal. Kyiv had tried twice to blow it up – with a truck bomb in 2022, and a sea drone the following year.

pg:https://www.pbs.org/newshour/science/.desc: It's the little space probe that could: Nearly 50 years after it was launched, NASA's Voyager 1 on Wednesday became the first human-made object to travel one light-day — or 16 billion miles — away from Earth.
paras: It's the little space probe that could: Nearly 50 years after it was launched, NASA's Voyager 1 on Wednesday became the first human-made object to travel one light-day — or 16 billion miles — away from Earth.

Voyager 1 and its sister spacecraft, Voyager 2, set off in 1977 on their mission to explore the solar system's giant planets – Jupiter, Saturn, Uranus and Neptune – and their moons. A rare planetary alignment at the time allowed NASA to chart a flight path that required minimal fuel, using the planets' gravity to slingshot the probes toward their destinations.

The twin spacecraft beamed dazzling, never-before-seen photos of the outer planets back to Earth and revealed many of their secrets for the first time — like the discovery that Jupiter's Great Red Spot is an enormous storm system.

paras: US President Donald Trump, Chinese President Xi Jinping and Russian President Vladimir Putin will hold a three-way meeting on Thursday in the southern Chinese city of Shenzhen, the first ever between the leaders of the world’s three most powerful militaries.

The meeting, which will take place on the sidelines of the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) summit, has drawn comparisons with the 1945 wartime Yalta conference at which the United States, United Kingdom and then-Soviet Union agreed on the post-war order. But those powers had been allied during a world war. Analysts say the three men meeting on Thursday are arriving with very different goals, and that few concrete outcomes can be expected.

The trilateral meeting is taking place on the sidelines of the APEC leaders’ summit, which China is hosting in Shenzhen on November 18 and 19. Trump travelled to China after attending the Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN) meeting in Manila.

As the “Parent Trap” actor noted in his caption, the two stars first worked together on 2010’s “Remember Me,” a romantic drama also starring Emilie de Ravin and Meghan Markle. With his statement, Brosnan joins stars including Pattinson’s “Tenet” co-star Elizabeth Debicki and former Bond villain Rami Malek in congratulating the “Twilight” actor on securing the role.

Pattinson’s announcement as the next Bond put an end to long-swirling rumors surrounding which actor would step into the role. Other stars in the mix included Callum Turner, Jack Lowden, Nicholas Hoult, Josh O’Connor, Tom Francis, Aaron Taylor-Johnson, Harris Dickinson and even Harry Styles. Denis Villeneuve will direct the forthcoming film from Amazon MGM.

paras: Pete Hegseth has unveiled a new military deal with Venezuela in his first visit since the January US military raid to capture President Nicolas Maduro. The visit comes amid growing unease in Venezuela about the US’s influence over the country’s sovereignty.

pg:https://www.theguardian.com/sport/202.desc: Australia captain’s manager says ‘there is nothing he hasn’t answered’, while former coach Darren Lehmann will take time to ‘work through each allegation’
paras: Pat Cummins is standing firm on his position around “sandpapergate” after Cameron Bancroft claimed Australia’s Test bowlers in South Africa in 2018 gave him feedback on his “work on the ball”.

The current Test captain’s response to the fresh allegations comes as David Warner said he supported Bancroft’s 4,000-word account of the tour of South Africa, which the former Australia player said he wrote after Cummins denied all knowledge of sandpaper being taken on to the field in Cape Town eight years ago.
Bancroft wrote that Cummins’ comments during a marathon press conference last Friday left him feeling “betrayed and alone”.

pg:https://www.straitstimes.com/business.desc: Anthropic raises US$81.3 billion in IPO, topping SpaceX’s record debut as the AI firm prepares to trade on Nasdaq. Read more at straitstimes.com.
paras: Anthropic PBC and its seven co-founders have raised US$81.3 billion (S$104.81 billion) in an upsized IPO, becoming the first frontier AI lab tapping the public markets to fund its development of thinking machines.

The artificial intelligence firm sold 956.4 million shares and the co-founders sold 23.6 million shares for US$83 each, according to a statement on Nov 18, above the marketed range. The company had marketed 801.4 million shares, while the co-founders offered 23.6 million shares, in a range of US$70 to US$78 each, according to its filings.
Pricing the shares above the range gives the company a fully diluted valuation of roughly US$1.5 trillion.

paras: The technology sector faces questions over whether huge AI investments will ever pay off, and has now been rocked by claims that Nvidia founder Jensen Huang had an affair with an alleged Chinese spy -- who might have funneled restricted chips to Beijing.

The scandal, along with reports that Huang had affairs with Nvidia employees, led to his resignation as chief executive last week, raising doubts about the prospects for one of the world's largest companies.
In its highly anticipated earnings release Tuesday, Nvidia said third-quarter revenue doubled to more than $115 billion, generating a net profit of $65.3 billion.

pg:https://www.skysports.com/cricket/new.desc: Cameron Bancroft backed up Usman Khawajas claims that the whole Australia team knew about the 2018 Sandpapergate, contradicting strong denials about it from Test captain Pat Cummins; Bancrofts lengthy statement added another twist to the ongoing scandal for Cricket Australia
paras: Pat Cummins' handling of Australia's Sandpapergate has been called into question, following Cameron Bancroft's explosive statement about the 2018 scandal.

Bancroft issued a 4,000-word statement on Wednesday insisting "the whole team" knew about plans to use sandpaper to tamper with the ball during the Test series against South Africa, supporting claims made by former team-mate Usman Khawaja.

The statement contradicts comments by Cummins during an extraordinary 68-minute press conference last week, where he forcefully denied renewed ball-tampering allegations, with Australian cricket rocked by conflicting reports from that series.

pg:https://www.kcra.com/article/californ.desc: Thousands of utility customers across California are without power Wednesday morning as strong weather conditions pass through the region.
paras: The KCRA 3 weather team issued an Alert Day for Northern California because of the safety risks posed by the expected rain, wind and snow.
PG&E said before 5 p.m. that power had been restored to 25,000 customers in El Dorado, Placer and Nevada Counties.

Customers can see real-time power outage information at PG&E’s online outage center. You can search for a specific address or look up the outages by city or county. PG&E said the site has been updated to include 16 languages.

pg:https://www.bbc.com/news/articles/cm8.desc: The head of Crimea said traffic was suspended after another attack on the link between Russia and the occupied territory.
paras: The Moscow-installed head of Crimea, Sergei Aksyonov, confirmed that traffic was temporarily suspended following another strike on the bridge connecting Russia to occupied Crimea.
The critical bridge had already been hit twice earlier in the week resulting in severe damage and part of the bridge collapsing into the water.
The important infrastructure has long been targeted by Ukraine because of its significance as a logistical and symbolic asset to Moscow's war effort.

pg:https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2.desc: Storm expected to move into southern California, with LA residents warned of potential evacuation orders
paras: Heavy rain pounded California’s Bay area, with record rainfall in downtown San Francisco and flooding and power outages across the region, as an “atmospheric river” arrived on Wednesday and dumped precipitation across the state.

The storm was expected to move into southern California on Wednesday night and Thursday, with Los Angeles warning residents in mudslide-prone areas of potential evacuation orders to come. Southern Californians were also warned of potential coastal flooding, heavy surf, wave damage to coastal piers and parking lots and beach sand erosion. Heavy snow warnings were issued for higher elevations of the Sierra Mountains, including in the Greater Lake Tahoe area.

Downtown San Francisco saw the most rainfall before noon in 76 years, at 2.11in, surpassing a record from 1950, the San Francisco Chronicle reported. By 3pm, Wednesday’s daily total of 2.28in had broken the record for the most rainfall on 18 November, which was previously set in 1918, the National Weather Service reported. South of San Francisco, in Santa Clara, there was flooding and standing water on several highways.

pg:https://www.independent.co.uk/sport/c.desc: Cummins attempted to kill off Sandpapergate for good with a bold hour-long press conference in Sydney, but his words only encouraged former teammates to speak out against him
paras: Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today.

There was an interesting digression during Pat Cummins’ 68-minute press conference last week, when he angrily pointed to Usman Khawaja’s claim that Australia wasn’t ready for “a brown captain” as the most egregious line in Khawaja’s new book. Perhaps, as the current Test captain, Cummins was genuinely offended. But it also served as a convenient way of pointing in another direction, painting Khawaja as an outsider, pitting Australia’s first Muslim Test player against the great institution of Australian cricket, as a man with an axe to grind.

It helped to pose a classic ‘your word against mine’ scenario. Cummins says unequivocally that he did not know Australia were ball-tampering in South Africa in 2018. Khawaja says “it was all of us” and tampering was openly discussed in changing rooms. Who should we believe?

pg:https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/1.desc: Musk says campaign cash alone cannot decide elections, even as he heavily funded Republican candidates in Texas.
paras: Elon Musk has said he feels “pretty foolish” about the amount of money he spent on this year’s US midterm elections after Republicans suffered sweeping losses.

Speaking virtually at The New York Times DealBook Summit on Wednesday, the CEO of Tesla and SpaceX and the world’s richest man said: “I feel pretty foolish about having spent so much money, and not seeing much for it.”
He added that Republican candidates might have fared worse without his spending, but that the outcome showed campaign cash alone could not decide an election.

pg:https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/1.desc: World court to issue key verdict in its first genocide ruling in more than a decade.
paras: The top court of the United Nations is scheduled to rule on whether Myanmar committed genocide against its Rohingya Muslim minority in a case brought by the West African nation of The Gambia.
The International Court of Justice (ICJ) in The Hague is to deliver its verdict on Thursday in what will be its first judgement on the merits of a genocide case in more than a decade.
Legal experts said the ruling could bear on South Africa’s ongoing case accusing Israel of genocide in Gaza, which Israel is contesting.

pg:https://www.theguardian.com/technolog.desc: The autonomous driving company suspended driverless taxi rides on US highways days after California banned the vehicles on its own freeways
paras: Waymo has stopped offering driverless taxi rides on freeways across the US indefinitely. The Alphabet subsidiary pulled its vehicles from highways nationwide after California banned them from freeways in response to recent traffic incidents.

Waymo had allowed riders to hail its robotaxis for freeway rides in the San Francisco Bay Area, Los Angeles, Phoenix, Miami and Austin. The California-based company offers rides on city streets in many other areas, including Las Vegas, Dallas and Denver. Those rides remain unaffected by suspended freeway service.

A Waymo spokesperson wrote in an email that the company has “temporarily restricted commercial freeway rides in all markets where we operate that service”, though it’s “continuing freeway testing with trained autonomous specialists behind the wheel”. The suspension was implemented last Wednesday, according to the spokesperson, but they didn’t say how long it would last.

paras: A pair of waterspouts were recorded recently in the San Francisco Bay area, much to the delight and shock of several observers, as storms pummelled the region.

pg:https://www.dw.com/en/grand-theft-aut.desc: After 13 years of waiting, fans around the world will get to play the latest installment in the blockbuster video game series. In focus: A tale of crime and violence in a fictionalized version of Miami.

paras: The International Court of Justice (ICJ), the United Nations’ highest court, is set to rule in a landmark case accusing Myanmar of committing genocide against its Rohingya minority.

pg:https://www.theguardian.com/world/202.desc: Russian embassy reacts to use of missiles made by Dutch-based company in Tuesday’s Kerch bridge attack. What we know on day 1,730
paras: Russian embassy reacts to use of missiles made by Dutch-based company in Tuesday’s Kerch bridge attack. What we know on day 1,730

Russia’s embassy in the Netherlands has posted a statement asking if the Netherlands had openly joined ⁠the conflict ⁠in ​Ukraine after a Dutch-based company said its missiles ⁠were used by Kyiv in Tuesday’s attack on a Crimean bridge. A section ​of the Kerch bridge that ‌connects annexed Crimea and Russia was destroyed on Tuesday by waves of ⁠drones and missiles. Soon after, Destinus – a Dutch-headquartered startup – confirmed its Ruta cruise missiles ‌were the only foreign-made weapons used in the attack, a rare operational role for a western manufacturer in a significant long-range strike.

pg:https://www.theguardian.com/artanddes.desc: Chataigniers en fleurs (Chestnut Trees in Blossom), which was painted in 1890 in Auvers-sur-Oise, France, set a new record for the Dutch post-impressionist
paras: A Vincent van Gogh masterpiece sold for a record-breaking $190.4m (£144.9m, A$285m) on Wednesday after a dispute between the seller and the heirs of a previous Jewish owner who sold it in the Nazi era, Sotheby’s said.

Chataigniers en fleurs (Chestnut Trees in Blossom), which was painted in 1890 in Auvers-sur-Oise, France, set a new record for the Dutch post-impressionist and became the most expensive work auctioned off so far this season.

The previous auction record for a painting by Van Gogh was $117.2m for the 1888 work Orchard with Cypresses, sold at Christie’s in New York in November 2022. But the New York Times reported on Wednesday that another 1888 painting by Van Gogh, Le Zouave, sold for “around $190m” in a private transaction through Christie’s less than a year ago.

pg:https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c.desc: Châtaigniers en fleurs was painted in 1890 in the final two months of Vincent van Gogh's life.

pg:https://www.yahoo.com/entertainment/c.desc: Manni L. Perez once said her "biggest fear" was playing a "damsel in distress." Her character in the year's most-anticipated game is anything but helpless.
paras: Iconic female main characters have been a staple of video games from the beginning (see: Ms. Pac-Man, Samus Aran, etc.), but the presence of a complex, fully fleshed-out woman at the core of GTA 6's story represents a significant change for a franchise that has been accused in the past of treating female side characters as equal parts eye candy and cannon fodder.

In the lead-up to the game's release, most of its sprawling cast of voice actors had remained a mystery. That's still true of nearly all of its main characters. But the voice behind Lucia was seemingly confirmed on Tuesday when the Game Awards announced that Manni L. Perez had been nominated for Best Performance for her voice work in the game. GTA 6 received eight nominations in total, including Game of the Year.

The revelation came as little surprise to die-hard GTA fans, who had speculated for months that the little-known American actor was the voice behind one half of the game's core duo. GTA 6's story centers around Lucia and her boyfriend Jason, a pair of outlaws trying to make their mark in a cartoonishly criminal knockoff of Miami called Vice City. The actor who plays Jason is still unknown.

pg:https://www.aljazeera.com/opinions/20.desc: Their meeting could revive the dream of nuclear disarmament that Reagan and Gorbachev nearly realised 40 years ago.
paras: Some are calling it Yalta 2.0. We’d rather think of it as Reykjavik 2.0, while also welcoming some of the broader diplomatic breakthroughs and global reordering achieved at Yalta almost 82 years ago.

Dmitri Trenin, who directed the Carnegie Moscow Center for many years and is now president of the Russian International Affairs Council, wrote encouragingly: “The US president has mentioned that an unprecedented trilateral meeting… would make sense if it were focused on denuclearisation.” Trenin wrote this in Al Jazeera while explaining why Russia could play a helpful role in negotiating a new nuclear agreement between its Iranian ally and the United States.

While anything that might help end the dangerous, destructive, and potentially apocalyptic conflagration in Southwest Asia would be more than welcome, we think the leaders can and should aim even higher: Why not rekindle the spirit of the 1986 meeting between US President Ronald Reagan and Soviet leader Mikhail Gorbachev, at which they came within a hair’s breadth, arguably one word, of agreeing to eliminate not only all ballistic missiles, as Reagan originally proposed, but all nuclear weapons, as Gorbachev countered. Reagan replied, “Yes, all”, and Secretary of State George Shultz agreed. “Let’s do it,” he said.

paras: Xi didn’t come to greet Putin. Cai Qi met the Russian president at the airport. Cai is a member of the Chinese Communist Party’s Politburo and ranks only fifth among China’s top officials. Xi went to the airport himself to greet Trump at the foot of the plane’s stairs.

pg:https://www.theguardian.com/world/202.desc: Zoo staff tried a colonoscopy, vibration plate and other procedures to aid the hippo in passing the hat to no avail
paras: Fiona the hippo, one of America’s most famous zoo animals, has died after efforts to remove a knitted hat that she swallowed after it fell into her enclosure proved unsuccessful.

With surgery too risky for full-grown hippos such as nine-year-old Fiona, who weighed in the region of 2,500lb (1,113kg), veterinarians tried an alternative method of getting the hat to pass through her system.

The hat fell near Fiona when a visitor to the Cincinnati zoo tossed it in the air, after which it bounced off a ceiling fan and fell into the enclosure, according to the Associated Press. Fiona ate the hat and was initially asymptomatic.

paras: NASA says Voyager 1, the agency’s longest-operating and most distant spacecraft, reached a distance of one light-day from Earth on Nov. 18, 2026, marking a milestone nearly five decades after its 1977 launch.

pg:https://www.independent.co.uk/arts-en.desc: This record-breaking documentary finally arrives on British shores, and it’s every bit as bewitching as you’ve heard
paras: Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today.

In an interview last week, Lance Oppenheim, co-director of the hit, record-breaking documentary You Can See Everything, described the film’s ostensible subject, Theranos founder and convicted fraudster Elizabeth Holmes, as a “human optical illusion”. He’s got a point. Throughout You Can See Everything – or at least, throughout the sections in which she appears, filmed mostly in the month leading directly up to her imprisonment – Holmes, moon-eyed and taut-voiced, is a figure of total, mystifying opacity.

Holmes may indeed be the illusion, but she’s not necessarily the illusionist. The heart of You Can See Everything, 2026’s very best film, is a triangle: at one vertex you have Holmes, at another, her current partner, Billy Evans. At the third sits Nathan Fielder, the film’s other director, who spends weeks interviewing the couple, eventually moving in to live with them in the days before Holmes surrenders herself to a Texan prison.

pg:https://www.theguardian.com/commentis.desc: I don’t know how the film will make me feel, I assume bad. But I will take the psychic damage. I’ll do it for the culture
paras: I don’t know how the film will make me feel, I assume bad. But I will take the psychic damage. I’ll do it for the culture

I realise it’s only the most annoying people on Earth who say this sort of thing, but I’m going to bravely say it anyway: I am an empath. I have always felt in tune with other people’s emotions and can easily take them on. The emotion I am most intensely attuned to, the one that takes the strongest hold of my body when I see someone going through it? Embarrassment.

There is nothing I hate more than seeing a person embarrassed, even if it’s a person I don’t like. I have always been like this. I remember sitting in the cinema watching There’s Something About Mary, all of my friends dying over a scene where Ben Stiller gets his testicular skin stuck in his zipper in front of his crush. They were rolling in their seats while my insides were rolling around. I felt physically ill. I knew logically it was a funny scene, that a normal person would laugh at the plight of this poor boy and his ball skin, but my humour bone was being crushed in a vice grip, as it always is when embarrassment abounds.

pg:https://www.theguardian.com/film/2026.desc: Nathan Fielder’s intense close-range study of fraudster Elizabeth Holmes is as gripping as any thriller
paras: Peter BradshawThu 19 Nov 2026 10.00 GMTLast modified on Thu 19 Nov 2026 15.58 GMTShare Prefer the Guardian on Google Thrillingly reckless, deliciously irresponsible and as gripping as any thriller, this situationist docu-hybrid masterpiece from co-directors Nathan Fielder and Lance Oppenheim gets up close and personal with convicted fraudster Elizabeth Holmes. It was Holmes’s US biotech firm Theranos, run jointly with her then partner Sunny Balwani, which in 2003 notoriously claimed to have invented a little box that could diagnose all manner of illnesses from a single drop of blood, its corporate prestige pumped by credulous board members including George Schultz and Henry Kissinger.

Yet Holmes has now met her match, perhaps even her predatory-platonic love match, in the film’s presenter Nathan Fielder, who is basically the Aleister Crowley of modern documentary satire, the hilarious dark master of turning truth into fiction and back again. His film delivers an extraordinary twist at around the halfway mark, and readers wanting to preserve the shock had better bail out here.

What we get is an Olympic stare-out contest between two gladiators of the polite straight face. Fielder’s conversations with the equally pop-eyed Evans have the same tension. Who is going to lose their cool first? Holmes repeatedly insists that the technology works, by which she appears to mean that the technology has caused her to be certain in the present that it could and will work in the future; the theory is impeccable and all that remains is the small matter of getting whatever tech stuff they need to go in the little box.

pg:https://www.theguardian.com/environme.desc: The diplomatic battles shaping the future of climate action as Cop31 enters its final days
paras: Ajit NiranjanFri 20 Nov 2026 07.00 GMTLast modified on Fri 20 Nov 2026 07.02 GMTShare Prefer the Guardian on Google The end is in sight. If all goes as planned, countries as diverse as wealthy petrostates erecting new oil rigs and low-lying islands threatened by rising seas will reach an agreement tomorrow in Antalya, bringing the 31st UN climate summit to a close (though, as usual, the talks are likely to overrun).

But tensions – much like our global temperatures – are running high. A draft text that satisfies all the competing interests is a long way off, and negotiators are expected to argue into the night and then the weekend. On the table are the electrification of the global economy, the transition away from fossil fuels, and the response to the looming overshoot of the 1.5C (2.7F) temperature target. Deepening the divide are long-running disputes over who should pay what, and emerging fights over the fairness of the transition and assumptions in the underlying science.

I’ve been following the contentious climate talks from afar every day for our liveblog, as my tireless colleagues on the ground have raced from interview to interview. The three big issues frustrating diplomats help the rest of us make sense of how well humanity is doing at keeping the planet habitable.

pg:http://obernolte.house.gov/media/pres.desc: WASHINGTON, D.C. – Congressman Jay Obernolte (CA-23) announced today that his bipartisan Preventive Health Savings Act (H.R. 4464), legislation to modernize how Congress evaluates the long-term fiscal impact of preventive health care policies, has passed the U.S. House of Representatives.
paras: WASHINGTON, D.C. – Congressman Jay Obernolte (CA-23) announced today that his bipartisan Preventive Health Savings Act (H.R. 4464), legislation to modernize how Congress evaluates the long-term fiscal impact of preventive health care policies, has passed the U.S. House of Representatives.

Led by Rep. Obernolte and Rep. Diana DeGette (CO-01), the Preventive Health Savings Act will allow the Congressional Budget Office (CBO) to evaluate the potential long-term savings of preventive health care legislation over a 30-year period. Currently, CBO primarily evaluates legislation within a 10-year budget window, which can overlook savings from policies that prevent chronic diseases, reduce the need for costly medical treatments, or improve long-term health outcomes.

By providing Congress with a more complete understanding of the potential long-term savings associated with preventive care, the legislation aims to support evidence-based health care policies that improve patient outcomes while reducing future federal health care expenditures.

pg:https://news.illinois.edu/is-the-proj.desc: Illinois expert addresses the public health impacts of U.S. Army’s planned detonation of lead explosives.
paras: CHAMPAIGN, Ill. ­— On Monday, Nov. 23, the U.S. Army plans to conduct two controlled detonations of degraded lead azide explosives in Middletown, Iowa, generating a plume spreading lead dust across eastern Iowa and western Illinois. Dr. Will Sander, a professor of preventive medicine and public health at the University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign, spoke with News Bureau Biomedical Sciences Editor Liz Ahlberg Touchstone about what the detonation could mean for public health, and what precautions residents can take both during the event and in the aftermath.

There is a mild public health concern, particularly for young children. There is no acceptable level of lead exposure for people, as defined by the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, and children are much more sensitive to lead due to the potential effects on brain development. Unfortunately, lead does not break down, so there is still some inherent risk no matter how long after the air plume occurs.

People in the potential area of air drift should stay inside as much as possible during the first 24 hours after the explosion to minimize risk. However, you can still go outside for short times as needed to take the dog out or get to the store.

pg:https://eos.org/research-and-developm.desc: Scientists and Iowa residents are planning to independently monitor lead levels in the air and soil in the days before and after a planned detonation of lead azide, a military explosive, near Middletown, Iowa on Monday.
paras: The stockpile of lead azide, held at the Iowa Army Ammunition Plant in Middletown, has been deemed unsafe to transport by the U.S. Army. The Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) granted an emergency permit to the U.S. Army based on the explosion risk, saying that the condition of the lead azide “presented an imminent and substantial threat to human health and the environment.”

Maps released by the U.S. Army this week showed that a plume of lead-containing dust could travel roughly 100 miles from Middletown in the hours after the detonation. However, new official maps of the plume were not updated following an announcement that the detonation, originally scheduled for Friday, had moved to Monday.

That’s left scientists and communities with just days to make plans to monitor the plume’s impacts. “These are tough circumstances to plan sampling campaigns under,” said University of Iowa environmental scientist David Cwiertny, who is leading an effort to track lead levels in the environment both before and after the detonation. “But we’ll do what we can.”

pg:https://movieweb.com/gta-6-lucia-twis.desc: It was bound to stir up controversy eventually.

Previous games have been torn apart by people who believe they glorify violence, romanticize criminality, and encourage general lawlessness, but that's not the criticism currently swirling around Rockstar's latest release.

A few gamers are instead rankled at the fact that, early in the story, the game's female protagonist displays a heavily questionable parenting choice. One gamer, who goes by @squidlord on X, said they lost interest in GTA 6 after a plot line within the first 30 minutes of gameplay gave them "such a visceral reaction there was no way I was ever going to be back on board to support dealing with them."

The upset these gamers express is interesting, considering its source. It's almost as if they've forgotten what franchise they're playing. For those who've never enjoyed the GTA games, it seems important to point out how extreme some of the storylines within them can get. In GTA 5, for example, there is an unskippable, necessary plot line in which one of the protagonists quite willingly tortures a man for information.

pg:https://www.avclub.com/game-theory-gr.desc: Grand Theft Auto VI and The Game Awards deserve each other
paras: The current reason I’m feeling like a frog slow-boiling in the warm waters of a fictitious, it-took-human-beings-10-million-hours-of-computer-drudgery-to-model Florida city, though, is that other tentpole event sticking out of end of the annual gaming calendar, like a piece of rebar lodged in Phineas Gage’s head: The Game Awards. After all, it was Tuesday morning when Geoff Keighley’s celebration of video game commercials (with the occasional trophy, or dollop of supposed activism, thrown in) announced that GTA VI had been nominated for Game Of The Year, despite, again, the total number of people who’d played it at that point likely not breaking a thousand.

I’m not suggesting any kind of impropriety here, mind you; the critics who voted for the game’s nomination are probably from the major outlets that have played it—and even if they weren’t, I’m open to the idea that Grand Theft Auto VI should have a GOTY nomination locked down from this particular body, basically by default. Because, honestly, GTA and The Game Awards deserve each other.

You can argue, as I imagine Keighley would, that this kind of communal interest is a net benefit to gaming, creating a force of attention so large that not even our collective cultural gatekeepers can deny it. (Because, god, but is there nothing that a certain kind of gaming brain can’t stand then to be casually dismissed by The New York Times.) Meanwhile, those of us on the skeptic side can point to all the ways the TGAs do what monocultures always do, i.e., grind down massive amounts of diversity and varied experiences into a uniform nubbin while extracting as much cash from folks as humanly possible.

But I believe it’s way more likely that they are starting again as though nothing has happened, like it’s a multiverse in a Marvel movie where old or dead or alternate versions of superheroes just turn up and do their thing.”

Questions had been asked before over the future of the Bond character, particularly after it was revealed in the run-up to No Time to Die in 2019 that the 007 codename was to be given to Lashana Lynch’s new MI6 agent Nomi. Was Bond really about to be put out to pasture? The ambiguity of the future of Bond – which was seen by some as a new front in the culture war – was underscored by Craig’s open dislike of the role, and his determination that No Time to Die was his last film in the role.

Vaines suggests that the Bond death narrative was Craig’s way of making sure he never had to come back to a series that, at that time, was still under the control of its original production company Eon. “I believe Daniel Craig wanted a definitive line drawn under his Bond, which everyone agreed on at the time. The Eon team may well have just planned to effectively start again the way that rather good opening sequence in the first Craig Bond played out, establishing after two kills that he was an 00 agent. pg:https://www.cnn.com/2026/11/21/tech/a.desc: A mathematician who works for artificial intelligence giant Anthropic claims he has solved a Holy Grail of math problems with the help of the company’s AI tool Claude.
paras: It marks the second time in recent months that an AI company or someone linked to one claims to have cracked a famed unsolved math problem.

Levent Alpöge, a member of the company’s technical staff, made the announcement Friday by way of a four-page explanation posted on his website. He said that he believes by working with Claude, he has found a proof of the Riemann Hypothesis.

paras: New Delhi: Negotiations at the UN climate summit in Turkey extended into “extra time” on Saturday, as consensus on the outcome document remained elusive amid deep divisions among nations over how the text should address fossil fuel emissions in an increasingly warming world, while also taking into account the Global South’s demand for economic growth.

Negotiators worked through the night to try to break the deadlock over energy, finance and science, as the summit went past its scheduled closing time on Friday without an agreement. Saudi Arabia, Russia and India are among the countries understood to have opposed any decisive reference to the “phase-out of fossil fuels” in the text.

From the outset of the 31st Conference of the Parties (COP31) to the UN Framework Convention on Climate Change, references to fossil fuels remained central to the deadlock, pushing the summit into overtime.

Scores of countries ended the week-long U.N. conference on weapons by agreeing to "elaborate" a possible accord on such lethal autonomous weapons systems by 2028. But they didn't commit to binding rules sought by U.N. Secretary-General António Guterres, many countries, and activists.

pg:https://www.npr.org/2026/11/21/nx-s1-.desc: U.N. talks in Geneva have failed to deliver binding rules on autonomous weapons, as humanitarian groups warn that military AI is advancing far faster than diplomacy.

paras: UNITED NATIONS (AP) — Rights groups are calling for military and economic sanctions against Myanmar after the United Nations' highest court, in the first ruling of its kind, determined that its government committed genocide against the Rohingya minority in a brutal 2017 military operation.

The International Court of Justice has no power to enforce Thursday's ruling, which orders Myanmar's military-supported government to allow those who fled the violence to return home safely, to pay reparations to the Rohingya Muslims and prosecute those suspected of having committed genocide.

Myanmar's government has denied committing genocide, claiming it acted against insurgents, and is considered unlikely to fulfill any of the court's demands. President Min Aung Hlaing, the former military leader, was in charge of the 2017 operation. The court said evidence showed Myanmar forces killed about 100,000 Rohingya.

pg:https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2.desc: Anticipating flood of Democratic requests, US president issues executive order in attempt to stymie oversight efforts
paras: Donald Trump is directing federal contractors and subcontractors to consult with his administration about inquiries they receive from Congress and to withhold any communications that the White House considers privileged, according to an executive order issued late Friday.

The companies must also coordinate with the White House and US agencies on “appropriate responses” to any such requests, the order says. If they fail to comply, the White House warns, their contracts could be terminated and their future work with the federal government suspended.

Democrats have made government contracts one of their top investigative targets , noting that federal money has been flowing to companies linked with Trump’s family, particularly at the Pentagon.

pg:https://theconversation.com/cop31-why.desc: Negotiations broke down over whether to directly address fossil fuels, leaving the most climate-vulnerable nations deeply disappointed.
paras: The UN’s annual two-week climate summit, Cop31, has ended in failure. Countries could not find consensus on a final agreement. It is the first such failure in more than 20 years.

The summit started relatively smoothly. In fact, the conference agenda was adopted within a few hours on day one, as country parties found nothing objectionable. At the time, this event looked like it might be smooth sailing: another summit simply focused on implementing policies agreed in previous years.

But week two became explosive. First, the draft agreement – which if adopted would have been known as the Antalya Accords – conceded that we have failed to keep global temperature rise below 1.5˚C and that the world is entering a period of “overshoot”. Second, oil and gas producing nations fought to keep the root cause of climate change – namely fossil fuels – out of any deal. And they succeeded, as the agreement fell through.

pg:https://time.com/article/2026/11/23/c.desc: Don't confuse the lack of another global accord with the lack of international engagement to tackle climate change.
paras: Participants sleep under COP31 signage in the main hall on the final day of the COP31 UNFCCC Climate Conference on Nov. 20 in Antalya, Turkey.

In the eleven years since the Paris Agreement, countries around the world have met annually to plot out the global consensus on how to tackle climate change. In some years negotiations led to big breakthroughs. In others, talks simply kept the ball in play, signaling to the world that nations were aligned in their desire to tackle climate change, even if it’s hard to agree on the exact path forward.

So it was a striking moment in the three-decade arc of United Nations climate negotiations when talks fell apart in Turkey over the weekend at this year’s COP31. The decade-long global consensus about the urgency of tackling climate change that produced the Paris Agreement at COP21 in 2015, it seems, came to an end on Sunday. The issues at play were many, of various levels of complexity, but the biggest was rather simple: a group of countries led by Saudi Arabia and Russia resisted reference to phasing out fossil fuels in the final text, and a bloc of 130 countries including the European Union refused to sign on without it.

paras: Add Defector to Google 131CommentsI did not imagine that the release of Grand Theft Auto VI would have any meaningful impact on my life, for the simple reason that I am not a gamer. I know and even respect a few people for whom video games are important, but I mainly regard this in the same way I do friends who really like square dancing, or go to church: nice for them, but not really my business.

While I have, in the past, dated gamers and even come to occasionally enjoy watching them play video games, that was mainly because I'm bossy and liked telling them Go over there, or Open that box, I bet there's something inside. Backseat driving a video game can be fun, but only insofar as I can manipulate what's happening. The appeal of Twitch, where you are simply one of dozens or hundreds of spectators watching someone else play a game, has always been totally, utterly alien to me. This would be true even without the dangers of encountering slurs in a chat or being confronted by the ever-present sight of anything that could be reasonably called "a gaming rig." No thank you.

And yet, I have found my conviction wavering recently as I find myself strangely compelled to click on clip after clip of people playing GTA VI. It started innocently enough, as people kept insisting that this game was teaching men to be thoughtful partners. I watched clips of people doing things Lucia will appreciate: buying groceries, taking her shopping, picking up flowers. I watched a guy make thoughtful decisions about how she might like to wear her hair. Soon I'd moved on to following along as people make Jason lovingly turn their house into a home, or invite Lucia to take the driver's seat on an aquatic adventure.

pg:https://www.dw.com/en/cop-deadlock-pr.desc: COP31 has been branded a failure after countries couldn't reach a final agreement, divided over a reference to "fossil fuels." But was the decision to walk away from a watered-down text actually a show of strength?

paras: It hasn't happened since 2009: International talks to fight climate change ended without any new pledges and commitments.

The summit, held this year in Antalya, Turkey, and known as COP31, was overshadowed by geopolitical tensions and wars, the withdrawal of U.S. President Donald Trump from the United Nations process to tackle climate change and growing alarm over the accelerating pace of global warming.

On Sunday, with the faltering talks already in overtime, the EU delegation walked out of the negotiations and said it could not accept a final declaration that did include language over the need to transition away from fossil fuels. The United Kingdom and many developing nations also rejected the proposed text as unacceptable.

pg:https://www.aljazeera.com/opinions/20.desc: The failure exposes a diplomacy that protects fossil-fuel power while leaving vulnerable countries to pay the price.
paras: COP31 ended without an overarching agreement on Sunday in Antalya, Turkiye, after nearly 200 countries failed to agree on a final climate pact. The proposed text could not even name the principal cause of global warming: fossil fuels. The European Union, several Pacific island states and other governments rejected it, while oil-producing countries resisted stronger language. After three decades of annual summits, this was the first such breakdown since 2009.

It is tempting to call this an extraordinary diplomatic failure. But the collapse reveals something more enduring. Climate negotiations have become remarkably effective at keeping governments at the table while avoiding the economic changes that meaningful climate action requires. The system is not designed literally to produce no agreements; it is designed to accommodate interests powerful enough to prevent decisive ones.

Consider what happened in Antalya. The EU objected that the final draft did not even mention fossil fuels. Yet the omission was not a clerical oversight. Earlier language on moving away from oil, gas and coal had been weakened as negotiations proceeded. The summit could not agree on how to implement the agreement reached at COP28 in Dubai in 2023 to transition away from fossil fuels in energy systems. What should have been the starting point for action became the point at which diplomacy broke down.

But the outcome on Sunday was even worse than expected — a failure to reach an overall agreement on fighting climate change at a time of frequent extreme weather events fueled by rising temperatures.

Gaining traction at this year’s summit, known as COP31, was always going to be difficult. Leaders and everyday people alike have plenty to contend with in addition to extreme weather, from wars to shaky economies to fears about artificial intelligence. Last year’s climate conference in Brazil, which had all the ingredients for a historic outcome, turned out to be a flop. And for the second year in a row, the United States, the world’s richest country and historically No. 1 polluter, did not take part; the Trump administration has pulled the U.S. from climate negotiations.

Still, there was hope, among lifetime environmental campaigners, climate scientists and negotiators from many countries, that there would be some progress on confronting the main cause of climate change: coal, oil and gas.

The climate talks, called COP31, ended Sunday in division and finger-pointing, without the hoped-for overarching agreement on fighting climate change that the world could follow. pg:https://apnews.com/article/climate-ch.desc: Going into this year’s U.N. climate talks in Turkey, expectations were notably low. Still, the outcome was even worse than expected—a failure to reach an overall agreement at a time of frequent extreme weather events fueled by climate change.
paras: United Nations climate talks in Turkey have failed to reach an overarching agreement due to disagreements over mentioning fossil fuels. The two-week negotiations known as COP31 ended Sunday without a main agreement. (AP Video/Aya Diab)

NEW YORK (AP) — Going into this year’s U.N. climate talks in Turkey, expectations were notably low. But the outcome on Sunday was even worse than expected — a failure to reach an overall agreement on fighting climate change at a time of frequent extreme weather events fueled by rising temperatures.

Gaining traction at this year’s summit, known as COP31, was always going to be difficult. Leaders and everyday people alike have plenty to contend with in addition to extreme weather, from wars to shaky economies to fears about artificial intelligence. Last year’s climate conference in Brazil, which had all the ingredients for an historic outcome, turned out to be a flop. And for the second year in a row, the United States, the world’s richest country and historically No. 1 polluter, did not take part; the Trump administration has pulled the U.S. from climate negotiations.

paras: A joint research team from Australia's University of Southern Queensland and Japan's Kindai University published a paper with these findings on the 23rd in the Monthly Notices of the Royal Astronomical Society. Patryk Sofia Lykawka, an associate professor at Kindai University who led the study, said, "Imagine discovering, after decades of mapping the solar system, that another planet had been hiding there all along." He added, "If PX2 exists, it could change our understanding of the solar system's history and why the most distant objects move in such peculiar orbits."

In the outer solar system, icy bodies are spread widely beyond Neptune. Many are concentrated in the Kuiper Belt, about 38–50 astronomical units (AU; 1 AU is the average Earth–Sun distance of about 150 million km) from the Sun. The problem is that over the past two decades, objects with highly elongated or steeply inclined orbits have been discovered much farther out. It has been pointed out that the gravity of known planets, including Neptune, alone cannot easily explain their movements.

A representative case is Sedna. This body travels around the Sun on a long, elliptical orbit and stays far beyond Neptune's orbit even at its closest approach to the Sun. The gravity of known planets alone cannot easily explain how such an orbit formed. An alternative hypothesis to explain this is "Planet Nine," a hidden giant planet with 5–10 times Earth's mass.

paras: It was a day-and-a-half past the official deadline when the UN climate summit COP31 began to unravel in earnest.

On Sunday morning, the corridors inside the huge expo-style venue in the Turkish city of Antalya were almost empty. Tired groups of delegates and media sat propped against the walls waiting for updates, charging their phones and drinking coffee. Many had barely slept. Australian Energy Minister Chris Bowen – who headed up the COP31 negotiations – reportedly slept for only a few minutes on the final night, as delegates kept waking him.
The talks dragged well into overtime to become the longest summit on record. But it would not finish the way co-presidents Bowen and Turkish Environment Minister Murat Kurum had hoped.

pg:https://www.npr.org/2026/11/22/nx-s1-.desc: Some 200 countries gathered in Antalya, Turkey, for COP31, the annual climate negotiations. Countries failed to reach an agreement over fossil fuels - the primary driver of global warming.
paras: COP31 President Murat Kurum, center, leaves a closing plenary session at the U.N. Climate Summit, Sunday, Nov. 22, 2026, in Antalya, Turkey. Nearly 200 countries failed to reach an agreement on whether they should move away from fossil fuels like coal and natural gas. Khalil Hamra/AP hide caption
ANTALYA, Turkey – International climate talks in Antalya, Turkey, broke down in overtime hours with a disagreement over how to address fossil fuels, the main cause of global warming.

On Sunday, delegates from nearly 200 countries failed to reach an overall agreement covering targets for electrification, finance to help developing countries adapt to the impacts of climate change, and how to respond to the fact that the planet will soon breach a key warming threshold.

pg:https://www.pbs.org/newshour/world/th.desc: While negotiations collapsed over one main point of contention — whether to include language about fossil fuels, the main driver of global warming — this fight over this has been building for many years.
paras: NEW YORK (AP) — Going into this year's U.N. climate talks in Turkey, expectations were notably low. But the outcome on Sunday was even worse than expected — a failure to reach an overall agreement on fighting climate change at a time of frequent extreme weather events fueled by rising temperatures.

Gaining traction at this year's summit, known as COP31, was always going to be difficult. Leaders and everyday people alike have plenty to contend with in addition to extreme weather, from wars to shaky economies to fears about artificial intelligence. Last year's climate conference in Brazil, which had all the ingredients for an historic outcome, turned out to be a flop. And for the second year in a row, the United States, the world's richest country and historically No. 1 polluter, did not take part; the Trump administration has pulled the U.S. from climate negotiations.

Still, there was hope, among lifetime environmental campaigners, climate scientists and negotiators from many countries, that there would be some progress on confronting the main cause of climate change: coal, oil and gas.

pg:https://www.dailymaverick.co.za/artic.desc: COP31 started with a sputter and ended in a puff of smoke as almost 200 countries failed to overcome divisions and reach a new deal on how to tackle climate change.…
paras: COP31 started with a sputter and ended in a puff of smoke as almost 200 countries failed to overcome divisions and reach a new deal on how to tackle climate change.
The conference was meant to conclude on Friday, but it ran well into the weekend as impasses over fossil fuels and finance turned COP31 into the longest climate conference ever.

The Antalya pact, drafted by the Turkish and Australian joint presidencies and the deal countries would have accepted had consensus been reached, called on countries to minimise the 1.5°C overshoot, which scientific reports have found is inevitable. The pact also called on developed countries (the EU, UK), historically responsible for higher emissions fuelling the climate crisis, to provide fair finance to developing nations to help them adapt to the impacts of climate change. The pact also invited countries to electrify their economies.

paras: Malaysia says it will send thousands of migrants and refugees back to Myanmar, despite acknowledging that many asylum seekers in the country had been victims of “atrocities” carried ​out by the junta in Naypyidaw.

paras: The US army has released new maps showing the projected path of a toxic lead dust plume from the planned detonation of 68 barrels – five tons – of lead azide at an Iowa ammunition dump.
Projections show a plume moving south-west of the Iowa army ammunition plant in Middletown, stretching through a south-eastern portion of the state before extending into northern Missouri.

The army sent an emergency notification to cellphones on Tuesday confirming the time of the controlled explosion – and warning that some people within 5 miles south-west of the plant may be evacuated.
